name: THE JUDGE, THE JURY, AND THE LAWYERS
safetyNote: Nothing here is legal advice, and nothing here tells you what to do. It tells you who does what in a courtroom. Six of these questions say "in Michigan" because those rules are Michigan's own choice and other states do it differently. The rest are the same everywhere in the country.

questions.q: A jury in a Michigan court has just found you guilty. Who decides how long you go to jail?

options.explanation: The jury's job ended when it decided whether you did it. Picking the punishment is a separate job at a separate hearing.
The prosecutor can ask for a sentence. Asking for one and deciding it are two different things.
The two sides can agree on what to ask for. The judge still decides what the sentence actually is.

questions.hint: The jury already finished its job.
questions.principle: In Michigan the judge decides the sentence, even after a jury trial. This is one of the places where states differ. Six states, including Texas, let a jury decide the punishment in some felony cases, and in Texas the person on trial gets to pick which one does it. Michigan does not work that way.

keyPhrase.quote: The jury says whether. The judge says how long.
keyPhrase.gloss: Two jobs, two people.

scenario.setup: A school trip to the courthouse. A case just finished.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: The jury's part is over. They said guilty, and that's all they decide.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So when does he find out how long?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know a second hearing is coming and who runs it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You think the whole thing was decided this morning.

questions.q: You are on a jury and the room cannot agree on what the law means. What are jurors supposed to do?

options.text: Send the judge a written question.
Go with whichever lawyer explained it better.
options.explanation: Lawyers argue. What a lawyer says about the law is an argument, not the rule the jury has to follow.

options.text: Vote on what the room thinks it means.
options.explanation: A jury applies the law to the facts. Deciding what the law means is not the jury's job.

options.text: Ask the bailiff to explain it.
options.explanation: The prosecutor is one of the two sides, so that would be one side setting the rules for the whole case.

questions.hint: Only one person in the building is allowed to answer that.
questions.principle: The judge gives the jury written instructions explaining the law that applies. If the room gets stuck, the question goes to the judge in writing, everybody sees it, and the answer comes back to the whole jury. It does not go to a lawyer, and it does not go to whoever walks past the door.

keyPhrase.quote: Jurors decide facts, not law.
keyPhrase.gloss: A stuck jury asks the judge, in writing.

scenario.setup: Your aunt got called for jury duty and is telling everyone about it.

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Somebody in the room kept saying the law meant something else.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Who settles that?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: She explains the jury sends the judge a written question.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You picture twelve people arguing it out with nobody to ask.

questions.q: You are watching a case from the seats and there is no jury in the room. What is a trial like that called?

options.explanation: A trial without a jury is a real trial with a real verdict. No jury is coming.
Lawyers can agree on a plea. They cannot agree on a verdict, because a verdict is a decision somebody has to make.
A trial without a jury is finished business, not a warm-up. Nothing moves anywhere.

questions.hint: The judge is sitting on something called the bench.
questions.principle: A trial without a jury is a bench trial, and it is a full trial with a full verdict. The judge does both jobs: deciding what happened and deciding the law. A person can choose a bench trial instead of a jury trial, and it is still open to the public either way.

keyPhrase.quote: No jury means the judge does both jobs.
keyPhrase.gloss: It is called a bench trial.

scenario.setup: Back row of a courtroom, watching a case with your cousin.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Where's the jury? I thought there'd be twelve people.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: There isn't one. She picked to have the judge decide it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You follow what is happening instead of waiting for a jury.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You spend the morning thinking the real trial has not started.

questions.q: Your Michigan case is going to trial with a jury. Which of these does the jury decide?

options.text: How long you go to jail.
options.explanation: In Michigan the judge sets the sentence at a separate hearing after the verdict.
The judge gives the jury the law in writing. The jury applies it.
A jury does not review the decision to charge. That was made long before by the prosecutor.

questions.hint: A jury answers one question, and it is a question about facts.
questions.principle: A jury decides one thing: whether the case was proved. Not the sentence, not the meaning of the law, and not whether the charge was a good idea. In Michigan a felony jury has 12 people and a misdemeanor jury in district court has 6.

keyPhrase.quote: One question, and it is about facts.
keyPhrase.gloss: Did it happen, and did this person do it.

scenario.setup: A summons came in the post for your uncle. The family is reading it.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: So if I do this, do I have to decide how long somebody goes away for?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No. That part's the judge.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He turns up knowing what he is actually being asked to decide.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He spends the week worrying about a decision that was never his.

questions.q: You want to explain your side to the judge before your hearing. When can the judge listen to you?

options.text: In court, with the other side there.
Any time, in the judge's office.
options.explanation: A private word with the judge about your case is exactly what the rule does not allow.
Going through a lawyer does not make a one-sided conversation allowed. The rule is about who is present, not who is speaking.
The judge does listen to you. It just has to happen in the open, with the other side there.

questions.hint: The rule is not about when. It is about who else is there.
questions.principle: A judge is not allowed to hear one side of a case without the other side present. The rule exists so nothing gets decided on something only one side knows about. You do get heard. It happens in the courtroom.

keyPhrase.quote: Both sides, or neither.
keyPhrase.gloss: A judge cannot listen to one person alone.

scenario.setup: A hearing you are watching. Somebody in the gallery stands up.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: Anything you want me to hear has to be said in here, with both sides present.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Why can't he just tell her outside?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You understand it is a rule, not the judge being difficult.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It looks like the judge refusing to listen.

questions.q: The judge in your case turns out to know your family from church. What is the judge supposed to do?

options.explanation: Quietly stepping off hides the reason from the people who needed to hear it.
The point is not whether anything went wrong. It is that both sides get to know and can say whether it worries them.

options.text: Ask your family to stay out of the courtroom.
options.explanation: The connection is what matters, not who is sitting in the seats.

questions.hint: The fix for a judge knowing somebody is not secrecy.
questions.principle: A judge who has a connection to somebody in a case is expected to put it on the record so both sides know and can say whether it worries them. Sometimes the judge steps aside and sometimes both sides are fine with it, and either way it happens in the open. The same idea runs through everything a judge does: nothing about your case happens where one side cannot see it.

keyPhrase.quote: A judge says it out loud.
keyPhrase.gloss: Connections get disclosed, not hidden.

scenario.setup: A hearing that has not started yet.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: For the record, I know this family from church. Either side may object.

lines.label: LAWYER
lines.text: No objection.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Everybody heard it, and nobody finds out later.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It comes out afterward and the whole hearing is in doubt.

questions.q: Which of these is the judge's job during your case?

options.text: Making sure the rules get followed.

options.explanation: A judge does not investigate. Each side builds and brings its own case.

options.text: Making sure guilty people get convicted.
options.explanation: That would make the judge a second prosecutor, which is not what the job is.

options.text: Making sure the prosecutor treats you fairly.
options.explanation: That would make the judge your lawyer. You already have one for that.

questions.hint: Everybody else in the room has a side. What is left?
questions.principle: A judge runs the process and applies the law. Not on your side, not on the state's side, and not out finding evidence. Our system puts each side in charge of building its own case and puts one person in charge of making sure it is done by the rules.

keyPhrase.quote: The judge runs the rules, not a side.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everybody else in the room has one.

scenario.setup: School trip. The class is watching a hearing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: The judge hasn't asked one question about what actually happened.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: That's not the judge's job. Both lawyers do that part.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know who to watch for the actual argument.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You wait all morning for the judge to dig into it.

questions.q: The prosecutor comes over in the hallway and offers to explain what happens next. Who does the prosecutor work for?

options.explanation: A prosecutor is one of the two sides. The neutral person in the room is the judge.
A prosecutor talks to victims and takes their views seriously. The victim is still not the client.
The prosecutor's office is separate from the court, with its own boss and its own budget.

questions.hint: Somebody brought this case. Who was it?
questions.principle: A prosecutor represents the government, which is why cases are called The People against somebody. In Michigan the job title is prosecuting attorney, elected by county. Most other states say district attorney, and television almost always says DA. Same job.

keyPhrase.quote: The prosecutor works for the state.
keyPhrase.gloss: Being friendly is not the same as being on your side.

scenario.setup: The hallway outside a courtroom. The prosecutor is being friendly to everybody.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: She's nice. Is she kind of neutral?

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: No, she's the other side. She's just polite.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You can tell being decent apart from being on your side.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You read good manners as a signal about the case.

questions.q: Somebody stole your bike and the case is going to court. What are you in that case?

options.explanation: The victim is the person it happened to, and that is not the same as bringing the case. The state brings it.
A prosecutor has a client, and the client is the government.

options.text: A party, the same as the defendant.
options.explanation: Police investigate and prosecutors charge. Separate offices, separate jobs, separate bosses.

questions.hint: Ask whose name the case is brought in.
questions.principle: A crime is treated as something done against the whole community, so the state brings the case and the person it happened to is a witness. That can feel wrong, since it happened to you. Michigan's Crime Victim's Rights Act gives victims real standing anyway, including being told what is happening and speaking at sentencing. What it does not do is make the victim the client.

keyPhrase.quote: The victim is a witness, not the client.
keyPhrase.gloss: The case belongs to the state.

scenario.setup: Somebody took your bike. A meeting at the prosecutor's office.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So you're my lawyer for this?

lines.label: PROSECUTOR
lines.text: No. I represent the state. You're a witness, and you can speak at sentencing.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know what to expect and what to ask for.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You think you have a lawyer, and later find out nobody was yours.

questions.q: You have been charged with a crime and you are at the courthouse with questions. Which of these people is allowed to give you legal advice?

options.explanation: The prosecutor is the other side of your case. The other side cannot advise you.
A judge decides your case. Advising you would put the judge on your side.
Court staff can explain what a form is and where it goes. They are not allowed to tell you what to do.

questions.hint: Advice has to come from somebody whose job is you.
questions.principle: Only a lawyer working for you can give you legal advice. In a criminal case the prosecutor is the other side, so that is not them. Court clerks are helpful and are not allowed to cross that line, which is why a clerk will explain where a form goes but not what to write on it. Worth knowing: prosecutors only handle criminal cases. If you are the one suing somebody, there is no prosecutor in that case at all, and the only person who can advise you is a lawyer you find yourself.

keyPhrase.quote: Advice comes from your side only.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everybody else can explain, not advise.

scenario.setup: The clerk's counter on the first floor.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Should I check this box or not?

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: I can tell you what the box means. I can't tell you what to pick.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know that is a rule, not a brush-off, and you find a lawyer.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You take a guess on a form that matters.

questions.q: The prosecutor tells the judge something that helps you. Why would the other side do that?

options.text: Because the job is to be fair, not to win.
Because the prosecutor has switched to your side.
options.explanation: A prosecutor can be fair to you and still be the other side. Both are true at once.

options.text: Because the case is about to be dropped.
options.explanation: Neutral is the judge's job, and nobody else picks it up partway through a hearing.

options.text: Because the judge made the prosecutor say it.
options.explanation: Saying something to the judge is just how court works. It does not change who a prosecutor represents.

questions.hint: Winning is not actually the prosecutor's job description.
questions.principle: A prosecutor is supposed to seek a just result rather than a win, and that duty includes telling the court things that help the other side. Doing that job well can look like friendliness or like a signal that things are going your way. Neither is what it is. The side has not changed.

keyPhrase.quote: Fair is not the same as friendly.
keyPhrase.gloss: And friendly is not the same as yours.

scenario.setup: A hearing you are sitting in on. It goes better than expected.

lines.label: PROSECUTOR
lines.text: For the record, this person has been at every hearing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Wait, is she helping him?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You understand a prosecutor is meant to be fair, and is still the other side.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You read one fair comment as the sides changing.

questions.q: The court gave you a lawyer because your family cannot pay. Whose side is that lawyer on?

options.explanation: Being appointed by the court does not make the court the client. The client is you.

options.text: The county's, since the county pays.
options.explanation: Who signs the cheque and who the client is are two different things.
An appointed lawyer has exactly one client, and it is the person being defended.

questions.hint: Ask who the lawyer has to keep secrets for.
questions.principle: An appointed lawyer is employed by the county and works for you. Those are two different things, and the second one is what matters. You get the same duties as somebody who paid: loyalty, confidentiality, and their best work. Michigan runs appointed defence through the Michigan Indigent Defense Commission, which sets minimum standards counties have to meet.

keyPhrase.quote: Paid by the county, working for you.
keyPhrase.gloss: Who signs the cheque is not whose side they are on.

scenario.setup: The kitchen. Your cousin's family is talking about the lawyer the court gave him.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: If the county's paying, whose side is she really on?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: His. That part doesn't change.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The family stops second-guessing the lawyer and starts helping.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Everybody treats the lawyer as an outsider.

questions.q: A friend tells you a court-appointed lawyer is not a real lawyer. What is a court-appointed lawyer?

options.text: A licensed lawyer, the same as any other.

options.explanation: Appointed lawyers are licensed, and many have more trial experience than lawyers you could hire.

options.text: Somebody from the court, not a lawyer.
options.explanation: Appointed counsel is a lawyer with a licence who works for you, not somebody employed by the court.

options.text: A lawyer you pick from a list.
options.explanation: You get a lawyer. Michigan courts have said you do not get to pick which one.

questions.hint: One of these is about who they are, not how they were assigned.
questions.principle: An appointed lawyer went to law school, passed the bar, and holds a licence. Michigan courts have said an indigent defendant is entitled to appointed counsel but not to counsel of their own choosing. You do get one. You do not get to shop.

keyPhrase.quote: Appointed is how you were assigned, not a kind of lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Same licence.

scenario.setup: The bus home from school.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Public defenders aren't real lawyers though.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: They passed the same bar exam as everybody else.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Your friend stops repeating it as if it were true.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Somebody who needs one goes in already convinced it is hopeless.

questions.q: You and your appointed lawyer keep disagreeing and you want a different one. What can you do?

options.text: Ask the court, and explain why.
Pick a different one from the county's list.
options.explanation: Paying the bill does not buy updates. Confidentiality runs to you.
The court appoints the lawyer and does not become the boss of that lawyer's work.

options.text: Fire your lawyer the way you would one you paid.
options.explanation: Loyalty does not split. One client, and it is you.

questions.hint: You can raise it. You cannot go shopping.
questions.principle: Michigan courts have said that somebody who cannot afford a lawyer is entitled to appointed counsel but not to counsel of their own choosing. You can ask the court for a different lawyer and you have to give a reason. Not liking the advice is usually not enough. A real breakdown in being able to work together is a different matter.

keyPhrase.quote: You get a lawyer. You do not get to shop.
keyPhrase.gloss: A real problem is worth raising with the court.

scenario.setup: A friend is complaining about the lawyer her family was given.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: We asked for a different one and they said no.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Did anybody tell the court why?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: She learns you have to give the court a reason, not just ask.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The family stays unhappy and nobody ever raises it properly.

questions.q: You are the defendant in a criminal case. Which person in the courtroom argues for you?

options.explanation: The judge runs the rules for both sides and argues for neither.
Family can be there and can speak at sentencing. They cannot argue your case.
You can choose to represent yourself, and by default there is a lawyer whose whole job is this.

questions.hint: Everybody in the room has one job. Which one is arguing for you?
questions.principle: One person in a courtroom has the job of arguing your side, and that is your defence lawyer. The judge is neutral, the prosecutor is the other side, and everybody else is staff. You can represent yourself if you choose to, and courts warn against it for good reason.

keyPhrase.quote: One person argues for you.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everybody else has a different job.

scenario.setup: School trip. First time in a courtroom, looking around.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: There's like eight people up there. Which one's for him?

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: The one sitting next to him.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know where to look and who does what.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Every person in the room looks equally official.

questions.q: In Michigan you are charged with a crime that could mean jail time, and there is no money for a lawyer. What happens?

options.text: The court appoints one for you.

options.explanation: Not being able to pay is the reason you get one, not a reason to go without.

options.text: You get one only if it is a felony.
options.explanation: In Michigan it turns on whether jail is possible, not on whether the charge is labelled a felony.

options.text: Your family has to find the money.
options.explanation: Nobody has to borrow money. That is the entire point of appointed counsel.

questions.hint: This is the criminal side of the courthouse.
questions.principle: Appointed lawyers exist for criminal charges only, and in Michigan the right applies whenever jail is a possible penalty, which is more generous than the constitutional minimum. The US Supreme Court in Scott v. Illinois set the floor at cases where somebody is actually jailed, so a state sitting at that floor gives less than Michigan does. This is a place where where you live matters.

keyPhrase.quote: A free lawyer is a criminal-case thing.
keyPhrase.gloss: And only when jail is on the table.

scenario.setup: Your uncle is telling the family what happened at his first court date.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: The judge asked if I wanted a lawyer and whether I could pay for one.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: And you can't. So what happened?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He explains the court appointed one before anything else happened.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You assume no money means going in alone.

questions.q: In Michigan you want the court to give you a lawyer. What do you have to show?

options.text: That you did not do it.
options.explanation: Whether you did it is the whole case. It has nothing to do with getting a lawyer.

options.text: That the charge is serious enough.
options.explanation: The court works out whether jail is possible. You do not have to argue the stakes.

options.text: That you tried to hire one first.
options.explanation: Somebody who can afford a lawyer is expected to hire one, so there is a question to answer.

questions.hint: The word is affordable, not innocent.
questions.principle: The test is money. Michigan court rules list what a court looks at, including income, what you own, and what you have to pay out. There is usually a short form. It is a financial question and nothing else, and answering it does not say anything about your case.

keyPhrase.quote: The test is money, not guilt.
keyPhrase.gloss: Nobody is asking what happened.

scenario.setup: Filling in a form at the counter before a hearing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Does it matter what he's charged with?

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: Not on this form. It's asking what he earns.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The money questions get answered and the lawyer gets appointed.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Somebody starts explaining the case on a form nobody reads for that.

questions.q: In Michigan, if you cannot afford a lawyer for a criminal charge, when do you ask for one?

options.text: Once a trial date is set.
options.explanation: Most of what matters happens long before a trial date exists.
A lawyer is most useful before decisions get made, not after they are already made.
The court is supposed to ask, and asking yourself is available whether or not anybody offers.

questions.hint: The earliest chance is a real answer here.
questions.principle: Michigan court rules require the court at arraignment to ask whether you want a lawyer and whether you can afford one. Arraignment is usually your first appearance and it is where the charge is read and bond is set, so it matters that somebody is on your side by then.

keyPhrase.quote: Ask at the first hearing.
keyPhrase.gloss: The court is supposed to ask you too.

scenario.setup: Watching a first appearance from the gallery.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: Are you asking for a court-appointed attorney?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's the first thing they ask?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know the earliest moment somebody can ask.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You think a lawyer only turns up nearer a trial.

questions.q: Nobody has charged you with a crime. Somebody is suing you over money you owe, and you cannot afford a lawyer. What does the court give you?

options.text: A free lawyer, the same as in a criminal case.
options.explanation: The right to an appointed lawyer is about criminal charges, not about money disputes.

options.text: A free lawyer if the amount is big enough.
options.explanation: The size of the claim does not switch on a right that is not there in the first place.
The deadline to answer keeps running whether or not you have a lawyer.

questions.hint: Nobody is trying to put you in jail here.
questions.principle: There are two different systems and they work differently. A criminal charge means the government is trying to punish you, and if jail is possible you get a lawyer. Being sued means somebody wants money from you, no jail is on the table, and no lawyer comes with it. More than half of American adults believe otherwise, and two thirds of people under 35 do. Michigan does appoint lawyers in a few civil situations, such as cases about taking children from a parent, so the line is criminal charges plus a short list.

keyPhrase.quote: No criminal charge means no free lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Being sued is not a criminal case.

scenario.setup: An envelope on the kitchen table. Somebody is suing over money owed.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: It says I have to answer in 21 days. Do I get a lawyer for this?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Not for this kind. Nobody's charging you with anything.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The answer goes in on time instead of waiting for somebody who is not coming.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The deadline passes and the other side wins by default.

questions.q: Your lawyer thinks you should take a deal and you do not want to. Who decides?

options.explanation: Advice is your lawyer's job. The choice is not.
The judge takes a plea. The judge does not choose it for you.
Your lawyer can disagree out loud and still has to enter what you decided.

questions.hint: Whose case is it?
questions.principle: Michigan's rules for lawyers say it directly: in a criminal case the lawyer must abide by the client's decision on the plea to be entered, on whether to give up a jury trial, and on whether the client testifies. Those three are yours. Your lawyer's job is to make sure you understand what you are choosing.

keyPhrase.quote: The plea is your call.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your lawyer advises. You decide.

scenario.setup: A courtroom drama is on. Somebody's lawyer just takes a deal for them.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can a lawyer even do that?

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Not in real life. That one's the client's call.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know which decisions belong to the person, not the lawyer.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You take the television version as how it works.

questions.q: Your lawyer does not ask a witness a question you wanted asked. Who decides how the trial gets run?

options.explanation: The big choices are yours. How to run the questioning is professional judgment.
The judge rules on objections. The judge does not decide either side's questions.
Paying buys you a lawyer, not control of the tactics.

questions.hint: Some calls are yours. This is not one of the three.
questions.principle: The plea, the jury waiver and whether you testify are your decisions. Which witnesses to call, what to ask, and what to object to are your lawyer's professional judgment. That split is written into the rules lawyers work under. A question you wanted asked may have been left out on purpose, and asking why is a fair conversation to have.

keyPhrase.quote: Three decisions are yours. The tactics are your lawyer's.
keyPhrase.gloss: Ask why, do not assume a mistake.

scenario.setup: A break in the hallway during a hearing you are watching.

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: Why didn't his lawyer ask about the messages?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Might be on purpose. That part's the lawyer's call.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know a missing question is not automatically a mistake.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You spend the hearing sure the lawyer forgot something.

questions.q: Which of these is your decision rather than your lawyer's?

options.text: Whether you get up and testify.

options.explanation: Which witnesses to call is professional judgment, and it belongs to your lawyer.
What gets asked is tactics. Also your lawyer's.
Nobody picks their judge. Cases get assigned.

questions.hint: There are exactly three decisions on your list, and one of these is on it.
questions.principle: Three decisions belong to the client in a criminal case: the plea, whether to give up a jury trial, and whether to testify. Everything else is the lawyer's professional judgment. This is the same in essentially every state, because the rule lawyers follow was adopted from the same model everywhere.

keyPhrase.quote: Plea, jury, testify.
keyPhrase.gloss: Those three are yours. The rest is your lawyer's.

scenario.setup: Your neighbour took a plea deal years ago and still talks about it.

lines.label: NEIGHBOUR
lines.text: Everyone kept telling me what to do. In the end it was my signature.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So the lawyer couldn't just decide?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know which calls belong to the person, not the lawyer.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You assume the lawyer runs everything.

questions.q: You tell your lawyer you want to plead not guilty and your lawyer disagrees. What does your lawyer have to do?

options.text: Enter whichever plea is better for you.
options.explanation: Your lawyer can say so loudly and on the record, and still has to enter the plea you chose.

options.text: Ask the judge to sort it out.
options.explanation: There is nothing to sort out. The rule already says whose call it is.
Disagreeing about a plea is normal and is not a reason for a lawyer to walk away.

questions.hint: The rule does not have an exception for when the lawyer disagrees.
questions.principle: The plea is the client's decision, full stop. A lawyer who disagrees is supposed to say so clearly, explain why, and then do what the client decided. A lawyer cannot walk away from a case just because a client would not take a deal.

keyPhrase.quote: Disagreeing is allowed. Overriding is not.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your lawyer says so, then does what you chose.

scenario.setup: A film on in the background. A lawyer just overrules a client on screen.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can they actually do that?

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Not with a plea. That one's the client's call, even if the lawyer hates it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know disagreeing and overruling are different things.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You take the film version as how it works.

questions.q: You tell your lawyer something you have not told anybody. Who can your lawyer tell?

options.text: The judge, if the judge asks.
options.explanation: A judge cannot order your lawyer to hand over what you said in confidence.

options.text: The prosecutor, when the two sides share evidence.
options.explanation: Sharing evidence between the two sides does not reach conversations between you and your lawyer.

options.text: Your parents, if you are under 18.
options.explanation: Your lawyer's client is you. Being under 18 does not hand your parents the file.

questions.hint: Ask who the lawyer's client is.
questions.principle: What you tell your lawyer to get legal help is confidential, and if you are under 18 that still holds, because the client is you and not your parents. There are a few narrow exceptions and they are not the ones people expect. A lawyer may speak up to stop somebody being killed or badly hurt, cannot help you lie to the court, and can defend themselves if you later accuse them of doing a bad job. A judge asking, a prosecutor asking and a parent asking are none of those.

keyPhrase.quote: Your lawyer keeps it.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not the judge, not the prosecutor, not your parents.

scenario.setup: Careers day. Somebody asks the question everybody wanted to ask.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: If someone tells you something, who can you tell?

lines.label: LAWYER
lines.text: Nobody, unless they say so. Not the judge, not the prosecutor, not their parents.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know what a lawyer is actually for.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Somebody holds back from the one person on their side.

questions.q: You call your mom from jail and talk about your case. What is different about that call compared to a meeting with your lawyer?

options.text: The call can be listened to.

options.explanation: The protection covers your lawyer. It does not stretch to family.

options.text: The call is private if you say it is.
options.explanation: Saying a call is private does not make it private.

options.text: Only the parts about the case are protected.
options.explanation: Nothing about the topic makes a call private. Who you are talking to is what matters.

questions.hint: Ask who is on the other end.
questions.principle: Jails record calls, and a recorded call can be listened to and used later. That is how jails operate rather than a rule written in a statute, and a recording usually plays at the start of the call saying so. Calls with your lawyer are meant to be treated differently. Everything else is not private, no matter who you are talking to.

keyPhrase.quote: Only lawyer calls are private.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everything else on that phone is recorded.

scenario.setup: Your uncle works at the courthouse and is explaining how calls work there.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: Every call out of that building is recorded. Everyone knows it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Even to family?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know the difference between a lawyer call and any other one.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Somebody assumes talking to family is private and it is not.

questions.q: Which of these conversations stays private?

options.explanation: A probation officer reports to the court. That is the job.

options.text: Talking to a friend about your case.
options.explanation: A friend can be asked about it later, and a friend can answer.
One to one does not mean off the record. The other side is still the other side.

questions.hint: Only one person in this list has a duty to keep your secrets.
questions.principle: Confidentiality is not about the room or how quiet the conversation was. It is about who the other person is and what their job is. Your lawyer has a duty to keep what you say. A probation officer has a duty to report. A friend has no duty either way and can be asked.

keyPhrase.quote: Privacy comes from the person, not the room.
keyPhrase.gloss: Only your lawyer has that duty.

scenario.setup: Two people on a wall outside school.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: You can tell me, I won't say anything.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: If it ever mattered, they could just ask you.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Your friend is never put in that position.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Your friend means it and gets asked anyway.

questions.q: You tell your lawyer you actually did it. What does your lawyer do next?

options.explanation: Confidentiality covers this. It is one of the main reasons the rule exists at all.
Defending somebody who did it is a normal part of the job, not a problem with it.
The plea is your decision. Knowing the truth does not move that.

questions.hint: Everything in this chapter about whose decision it is applies here too.
questions.principle: A defence lawyer's job is to hold the state to its proof, not to decide whether you are guilty. What you say stays confidential either way. There is one limit: your lawyer cannot help you lie to the court, so knowing the truth changes what your lawyer can put in front of a jury. It does not change whose side your lawyer is on.

keyPhrase.quote: Your lawyer keeps working either way.
keyPhrase.gloss: The job is the state's proof, not your guilt.

scenario.setup: A group chat argument about a true crime show.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: His own lawyer knew he did it. That should be illegal.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's the job. The state still has to prove it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You understand what a defence lawyer is actually for.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You assume a lawyer would walk out on the spot.

questions.q: You told police what happened and now you want the case dropped. Who decides whether that happens?

options.explanation: The case belongs to the state. Your view is taken seriously and it does not decide.

options.text: The officer who took the report.
options.explanation: An officer investigates. Whether a case continues is not the officer's call.
A judge rules on what is in front of the court. Dropping a case is the prosecutor's move.

questions.hint: Whose case is it, once it has been filed?
questions.principle: Once charges are filed, the case belongs to the state and not to the person it happened to. A prosecutor will usually want to know what a victim wants and will often weigh it heavily. It is still the prosecutor's decision, and a case can go forward even when a victim asks for it to stop.

keyPhrase.quote: The case belongs to the state.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your view counts. It does not decide.

scenario.setup: The kitchen, a week after reporting the stolen bike.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I said I don't want to press charges anymore.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: They said that's not up to us now.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know who to talk to and what asking can and cannot do.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You expect it to be over and a subpoena arrives.

questions.q: In Michigan an officer arrests you and names a charge at the scene. When does that charge become official?

options.text: As soon as the officer says it.
options.explanation: Police ask for a charge. A prosecutor decides what to bring, or whether to bring anything at all.

options.text: When you are booked at the jail.
options.explanation: Booking is paperwork about who is in the building. It does not create a charge.

options.text: When the judge reads it at your first hearing.
options.explanation: The judge reads the charge out. It arrived already decided by somebody else.

questions.hint: Being arrested and being charged are two separate steps.
questions.principle: In Michigan police bring a warrant request to the prosecuting attorney, who decides what to charge and whether to charge at all. This means people get arrested and never charged, and people get charged with something different from what an officer said at the scene. Officers can issue tickets directly for smaller things, so the split is not perfect, but for anything serious the prosecutor decides.

keyPhrase.quote: Arrested and charged are two steps.
keyPhrase.gloss: The charge is real when it gets filed.

scenario.setup: Kitchen table. Your uncle got a ticket last night.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: The officer said what I'm being charged with.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is that definitely it?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He waits for the prosecutor's decision instead of panicking early.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He spends three days certain of a charge that may change.

questions.q: In Michigan, how does somebody become the prosecutor for a county?

options.explanation: Michigan county prosecutors are elected, not appointed by the state.

options.text: The judges in that county pick them.
options.explanation: Judges decide cases. They do not choose who brings them.
Police investigate and prosecutors charge. The prosecutor's office is separate and elected.

questions.hint: The person deciding who gets charged is on a ballot.
questions.principle: Every Michigan county elects its prosecuting attorney, the same way it elects a sheriff. The person who decides who gets charged, who gets a deal, and who gets left alone is somebody voters put there, and can vote out. Most states elect prosecutors and a handful appoint them instead, so this is another place where where you live matters. The assistants in that office are hired, not elected.

keyPhrase.quote: Your county's prosecutor is elected.
keyPhrase.gloss: The charging power belongs to somebody on a ballot.

scenario.setup: A sample ballot on the kitchen table before an election.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Why is there an election for prosecutor?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Because that's the person who decides what gets charged around here.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know who holds that power and where it comes from.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You think charging decisions come from somewhere nobody can reach.
